Last update: November 18, 2026 FILM AND TELEVISION can be powerful media to encounter a country’s history and future. And for Taiwan, it was the fall of Kuomintang (KMT) martial law in 1987 that changed its artistic landscape forever . As the White Terror period crawled to its end, Taiwan’s filmmakers were finally free of decades of censorship and information control — deadly years where indiscriminate KMT arrests, jailings, and executions of dissenters and activists included artists, journalists, writers, students, and other creators. Soon, dramatic works began depicting once-forbidden themes and social commentary. A liberalized government would also provide public funding to stimulate new productions as well as to restore cinematic works and preserve historic film reels . posts.title: Chinese Comedy-Drama “Now I Met Her” Falls Flat With Its Male Gaze
posts.description: by Brian Hioe 語言: English Photo Courtesy of SDAFF This is a No Man is an Island film review written in collaboration with Cinema Escapist . Keep an eye out for more ! NOW I MET HER is a technically accomplished film. However, where the film falls short is that, despite excellent execution, the plot proves derivative and underwritten by a strong male gaze Specifically, the movie follows teenager Zhang Shiyi, who discovers his deceased mother’s diary on his 18th birthday. Zhang, who was raised by his father, is drawn into the tales of his mother’s adventurous past as depicted in the diary. Much of Now I Met Her , then, consists of flashbacks, detailing Zhang’s mother—Li Dongyu—through the course of three turbulent romances. Li first falls for an amateur dancer as a teenager and then helps him win a dance competition. posts.title: “Just Like Weather” Metafictionally Muses About a Hongkonger Couple’s Emigration to the United States
posts.description: by Brian Hioe 語言: English Photo Courtesy of SDAFF This is a No Man is an Island film review written in collaboration with Cinema Escapist . Keep an eye out for more ! ALLEN FONG’S Just Like Weather is a triumph. Mixing documentary and fiction, the movie follows Christine and Hung-nin, a Hong Kong couple seeking to emigrate to the US. In restoration, the film sees new life. Hung-nin wants to emigrate not only as a way of seeking better opportunities, but out of a sense of unease about Hong Kong. This is in part, but not only, due to the impending 1997 handover of Hong Kong from British to Chinese control. Increasing numbers of Hongkongers, including Hung-nin’s family, have consequently sought to move to the US. Photo courtesy of SDAFF Likewise, Hung-nin is driven to emigrate out of a desire to prove himself. Christine makes more than he does as a real estate agent and supports the family.
